idiom_name: state struct + consumer-supplied render callback (function pointer plus user data)
implementation_notes: C has no component runtime, no closures and no standard UI layer, so the pattern is the hand-written structure: a struct owns the state and the transitions, and the markup half arrives as a function pointer plus an opaque user-data pointer that the consumer's drawing code receives - pointers to functions are ordinary objects in C and are how callbacks are expressed. What replaces the classic component (and the prop getters of a dynamic language) is that explicit callback contract: the consumer registers how to draw and the struct only ever hands over state. Prefer a GUI toolkit's own model/delegate split when one exists, because re-implementing the markup half is where theming and accessibility work lives; and because nothing re-renders automatically, the struct must explicitly notify the consumer's paint entry point after every transition.
pitfalls: No reactivity comes for free: nothing re-renders unless the transition explicitly calls into the consumer's draw code, so a forgotten notify leaves a stale screen.
The user-data pointer's lifetime is a hand-written contract; a callback firing after the canvas or context is freed is a use-after-free.
Prop getters have no typed return in C, so the attribute/ARIA contract degrades to strings a consumer can silently omit - publish one props struct and document the required fields.
